q-343855.name: Question 1
q-343855.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}-3y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$
q-343855.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,-3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,=-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-2 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=0 \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n}=\frac{6}{n\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=\frac{4}{3},$ which means the constant term is given by

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Next, from the second equation, ${b}_{n}=\frac{9{a}_{n}}{n\pi }.$ Substituting this into the third equation, gives

$$
-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3(\frac{9{a}_{n}}{n\pi })=\frac{6}{n\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{18}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81}.
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{9{a}_{n}}{n\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{n\pi }\cdot (-\frac{18}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81}) \\  & =-\frac{162}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼\frac{2}{3} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{18}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{162}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation y′−3y=f(x), where the Fourier series of the 6-periodic forcing function is given by f(x)∼−2+∑n=1∞6nπsin⁡(nπx3).The Fourier series of a particular solution is
23

EXPLANATION

We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series: yp∼a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx3)+bnsin⁡(nπx3).

Now, we compute the derivative: yp′∼ddx(a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx3)+bnsin⁡(nπx3))∼0+∑n=1∞an⋅(−nπ3sin⁡(nπx3))+bn⋅nπ3cos⁡(nπx3)∼∑n=1∞−annπ3sin⁡(nπx3)+bnnπ3cos⁡(nπx3)

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp′ and yp into the equation: (∑n=1∞−annπ3sin⁡(nπx3)+bnnπ3cos⁡(nπx3))−3(a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx3)+bnsin⁡(nπx3))=−2+∑n=1∞6nπsin⁡(nπx3)

Rearranging the terms, we get −3⋅a02+∑n=1∞(bnnπ3−3an)cos⁡(nπx3)+∑n=1∞(−annπ3−3bn)sin⁡(nπx3)=−2+∑n=1∞6nπsin⁡(nπx3).

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system: {−3⋅a02=−2bnnπ3−3an=0−annπ3−3bn=6nπ

From the first equation, a0=43, which means the constant term is given by a02=23.

Next, from the second equation, bn=9annπ. Substituting this into the third equation, gives −annπ3−3(9annπ)=6nπ⇒an=−18n2π2+81.

Therefore, for an with n≥1, we have

bn=9annπ=9nπ⋅(−18n2π2+81)=−162nπ(n2π2+81).

Therefore, our particular solution is yp∼23+∑n=1∞−18n2π2+81⋅cos⁡(nπx3)+∑n=1∞−162nπ(n2π2+81)⋅sin⁡(nπx3).

q-343819.name: Question 2
q-343819.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}+3y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{{field-2}}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$
q-343819.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{2}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{2}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & \,+3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{3{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{a}_{n})cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n})sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3{a}_{0}}{2}=0 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{a}_{n}=0 \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n}=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

Next, from the second equation, 

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6}.
$$

Substituting this into the third equation gives

$$
-(-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6})\frac{n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n}=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\,⇒\,{b}_{n}=\frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)} \\  & =-\frac{4(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{4(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 3a02+∑n=1∞(bnnπ2+3an)cos(nπx2)+∑n=1∞(−annπ2+3bn)sin(nπx2)=∑n=1∞2(−1)nnπsin(nπx2).

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system: {3a02=0bnnπ2+3an=0−annπ2+3bn=2(−1)nnπ

From the first equation, a0=0.

Next, from the second equation, an=−bnnπ6. Substituting this into the third equation gives −(−bnnπ6)nπ2+3bn=2(−1)nnπ⇒bn=24(−1)nnπ(n2π2+36)

q-344058.name: Question 3
q-344058.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}-3y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$
q-344058.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,-3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,=-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-3 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=2,$ which means the constant term is given by

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=1.
$$

Next, from the third equation, 

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9})\frac{n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{9}\cdot (-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}) \\  & =\frac{18}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼1 & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, a0=2, which means the constant term is given by a02=1.

q-342229.name: Question 4
q-342229.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}-y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$
q-342229.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & \,-(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & \,\,=-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}-{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}-{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}-{a}_{n}=\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}-{b}_{n}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=2,$ which means the constant term is given by

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=1.
$$

Next, from the third equation, ${b}_{n}=-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}.$ Substituting this into the third equation, gives

$$
(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2})\frac{n\pi }{2}-{a}_{n}=\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{16}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}.
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{2}\cdot (-\frac{16}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}) \\  & =\frac{8}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼1 & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{16}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{8}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series: yp∼a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx2)+bnsin⁡(nπx2).

Now, we compute the derivative: yp′∼ddx(a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx2)+bnsin⁡(nπx2))∼0+∑n=1∞an⋅(−nπ2sin⁡(nπx2))+bn⋅nπ2cos⁡(nπx2)∼∑n=1∞−annπ2sin⁡(nπx2)+bnnπ2cos⁡(nπx2)

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp′ and yp into the equation: (∑n=1∞−annπ2sin⁡(nπx2)+bnnπ2cos⁡(nπx2))−(a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx2)+bnsin⁡(nπx2))=−1+∑n=1∞4n2πcos⁡(nπx2)

Rearranging the terms, we get −a02+∑n=1∞(bnnπ2−an)cos⁡(nπx2)+∑n=1∞(−annπ2−bn)sin⁡(nπx2)=−1+∑n=1∞4n2πcos⁡(nπx2).

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system: {−a02=−1bnnπ2−an=4n2π−annπ2−bn=0

From the first equation, a0=2, which means the constant term is given by a02=1.

Next, from the third equation, bn=−annπ2. Substituting this into the third equation, gives (−annπ2)nπ2−an=4n2π⇒an=−16n2π(n2π2+4).

Therefore, for an with n≥1, we have

bn=−annπ2=−nπ2⋅(−16n2π(n2π2+4))=8n(n2π2+4).

Therefore, our particular solution is yp∼1+∑n=1∞−16n2π(n2π2+4)⋅cos⁡(nπx2)+∑n=1∞8n(n2π2+4)⋅sin⁡(nπx2).

q-342203.name: Question 5
q-342203.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}+5y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$
q-342203.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))+{b}_{n}\cdot n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)) \\  & \,+5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({b}_{n}n\pi +5{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-{a}_{n}n\pi +5{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}=0 \\ {b}_{n}n\pi +5{a}_{n}=0 \\ -{a}_{n}n\pi +5{b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

Next, from the second equation, 

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{5}.
$$

Substituting this into the third equation gives

$$
-(-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{5})n\pi +5{b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{b}_{n}=\frac{5(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+25)}
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{5} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{5}\cdot \frac{5(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+25)} \\  & =-\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+25)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+25)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+\frac{5(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+25)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

q-342203.html:
Question 5
?
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation y′+5y=f(x), where the Fourier series of the 2-periodic forcing function is given by f(x)∼∑n=1∞(−1)nn2πsin⁡(nπx).The Fourier series of a particular solution is
−(−1)nn(n2π2+25)
−5(−1)nn2π2(n2π2+25)
(−1)nn2(n2π2+25)
−(−1)nn(n2π2+25)
5(−1)nn2π(n2π2+25)
−25(−1)nnπ2(nπ+5)
5(−1)nn2π(nπ+5)
5(−1)nn2π(n2π2+25)
yp∼∑n=1∞{(−5(−1)nn2π2(n2π2+25))(S0)}⋅cos⁡(nπx)+{(−25(−1)nnπ2(nπ+5))(S1)}⋅sin⁡(nπx)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series: yp∼a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx)+bnsin⁡(nπx).

Now, we compute the derivative: yp′∼ddx(a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx)+bnsin⁡(nπx))∼0+∑n=1∞an⋅(−nπsin⁡(nπx))+bn⋅nπcos⁡(nπx)∼∑n=1∞−annπsin⁡(nπx)+bnnπcos⁡(nπx)

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp′ and yp into the equation: (∑n=1∞−annπsin⁡(nπx)+bnnπcos⁡(nπx))+5(a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx)+bnsin⁡(nπx))=∑n=1∞(−1)nn2πsin⁡(nπx)

Rearranging the terms, we get 5a02+∑n=1∞(bnnπ+5an)cos⁡(nπx)+∑n=1∞(−annπ+5bn)sin⁡(nπx)=∑n=1∞(−1)nn2πsin⁡(nπx).

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system: {5a02=0bnnπ+5an=0−annπ+5bn=(−1)nn2π

From the first equation, a0=0.

Next, from the second equation, an=−bnnπ5. Substituting this into the third equation gives −(−bnnπ5)nπ+5bn=(−1)nn2π⇒bn=5(−1)nn2π(n2π2+25)

Therefore, for an with n≥1, we have

an=−bnnπ5=−nπ5⋅5(−1)nn2π(n2π2+25)=−(−1)nn(n2π2+25).

Therefore, our particular solution is yp∼∑n=1∞−(−1)nn(n2π2+25)⋅cos⁡(nπx)+5(−1)nn2π(n2π2+25)⋅sin⁡(nπx).

q-343878.name: Question 6
q-343878.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}+36y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$
q-343878.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+36({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Rearranging the terms to find a common denominator:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(36-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(\frac{324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients:

$$
\frac{{a}_{n}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}{9}=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}(324-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation y″+36y=f(x), where the Fourier series of the 6-periodic forcing function is given by f(x)∼∑n=1∞3(−1)nn2cos⁡(nπx3).

Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.

The Fourier series of a particular solution is
3(−1)nn2(324−n2π2)
3(−1)nn2(324−n2π2)

−27(−1)nn2(324−n2π2)

EXPLANATION

We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series: yp∼∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx3).

Now, we compute the derivatives: yp′∼ddx(∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx3))∼∑n=1∞−annπ3sin⁡(nπx3)yp″∼ddx(∑n=1∞−annπ3sin⁡(nπx3))∼∑n=1∞−ann2π29cos⁡(nπx3)

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp″ and yp into the equation and have ∑n=1∞−ann2π29cos⁡(nπx3)+36(∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx3))=∑n=1∞3(−1)nn2cos⁡(nπx3).

Rearranging the terms to find a common denominator: ∑n=1∞an(36−n2π29)cos⁡(nπx3)=∑n=1∞3(−1)nn2cos⁡(nπx3) ∑n=1∞an(324−n2π29)cos⁡(nπx3)=∑n=1∞3(−1)nn2cos⁡(nπx3).

Now, equating the cosine coefficients: an(324−n2π2)9=3(−1)nn2⇒an=27(−1)nn2(324−n2π2).

Therefore, our particular solution is yp∼∑n=1∞27(−1)nn2(324−n2π2)⋅cos⁡(nπx3).

q-343874.name: Question 7
q-343874.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-4y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$
q-343874.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)-4({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine coefficients, we obtain 

$$
-{b}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)=\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\,⇒\,{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{2}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

q-343874.html:
Question 7
?
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation y″−4y=f(x), where the Fourier series of the 2-periodic forcing function is given by f(x)∼∑n=1∞2n2sin⁡(nπx).

Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.

The Fourier series of a particular solution is
−2n2(n2π2+4)
1n2π2+4
−2n2(n2π2+4)
2n2(n2π2+4)
−2n(n2π2+4)
yp∼∑n=1∞{(−2n2(n2π2+4))(S0)}⋅sin⁡(nπx)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series: yp∼∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx).

Now, we compute the derivatives: yp′∼ddx(∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx))∼∑n=1∞bnnπcos⁡(nπx)yp″∼ddx(∑n=1∞bnnπcos⁡(nπx))∼∑n=1∞−bnn2π2sin⁡(nπx)

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp″ and yp into the equation and have ∑n=1∞−bnn2π2sin⁡(nπx)−4(∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx))=∑n=1∞2n2sin⁡(nπx).

Rearranging the terms, we get ∑n=1∞−bn(n2π2+4)sin⁡(nπx)=∑n=1∞2n2sin⁡(nπx).

Now, equating the sine coefficients, we obtain −bn(n2π2+4)=2n2⇒bn=−2n2(n2π2+4).

Therefore, our particular solution is yp∼∑n=1∞−2n2(n2π2+4)⋅sin⁡(nπx).

q-342349.name: Question 8
q-342349.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-9y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$
q-342349.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)-9({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+9)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients, we obtain 

$$
-{a}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+9)=\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}}\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+9)}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{\pi }{{n}^{3}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+9)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

q-342349.html:
Question 8
?
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation y″−9y=f(x), where the Fourier series of the 2-periodic forcing function is given by f(x)∼∑n=1∞πn3cos⁡(nπx).

Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.

The Fourier series of a particular solution is
−πn(n3π−9)
−πn(n3π−9)
−πn3(n2π2+9)
1n3π2(n2π2−9)
n+1n3π2+9
yp∼∑n=1∞{(1n3π2(n2π2−9))(S0)}⋅cos⁡(nπx)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series: yp∼∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx).

Now, we compute the derivatives: yp′∼ddx(∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx))∼∑n=1∞−annπsin⁡(nπx)yp″∼ddx(∑n=1∞−annπsin⁡(nπx))∼∑n=1∞−ann2π2cos⁡(nπx)

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp″ and yp into the equation and have ∑n=1∞−ann2π2cos⁡(nπx)−9(∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx))=∑n=1∞πn3cos⁡(nπx).

Rearranging the terms, we get ∑n=1∞−an(n2π2+9)cos⁡(nπx)=∑n=1∞πn3cos⁡(nπx).

Now, equating the cosine coefficients, we obtain −an(n2π2+9)=πn3⇒an=−πn3(n2π2+9).

Therefore, our particular solution is yp∼∑n=1∞−πn3(n2π2+9)⋅cos⁡(nπx).

q-343880.name: Question 9
q-343880.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-3y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$
q-343880.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})-3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))=3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}-3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})=3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=3 \\ {a}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}-3)=\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {a}_{n}=\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+27)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{27(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+27)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

q-343880.knowledge_point: Solving Second Order ODEs Given the Fourier Series of the Forcing Function

q-343885.name: Question 10
q-343885.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-6y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼6+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$
q-343885.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})-6(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))=6+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-6\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}-6)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})=6+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=6 \\ {b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}-6)=\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {b}_{n}=\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+54)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+54)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Question 10
?
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation y″−6y=f(x), where the Fourier series of the 6-periodic forcing function is given by f(x)∼6+∑n=1∞2(−1)n+1n3πsin⁡(nπx3).

Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.

The Fourier series of a particular solution is
−1

1
2

18(−1)nn3π(n2π2+54)
2(−1)nn3π(n2π2+54)
18(−1)nn3π(n2π2+54)
−18(−1)nn3π(n2π2+54)
18(−1)nn2π(n2π2+54)
yp∼{(−1)(S0)}+∑n=1∞{(2(−1)nn3π(n2π2+54))(S1)}⋅sin⁡(nπx3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series: yp∼a02+∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx3).

Now, we compute the derivatives: yp′∼ddx(a02+∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx3))∼∑n=1∞bnnπ3cos⁡(nπx3)yp″∼ddx(∑n=1∞bnnπ3cos⁡(nπx3))∼∑n=1∞−bnn2π29sin⁡(nπx3)

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp″ and yp into the equation and have ∑n=1∞−bnn2π29sin⁡(nπx3)−6(a02+∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx3))=6+∑n=1∞2(−1)n+1n3πsin⁡(nπx3).

Rearranging the terms, we get −6⋅a02+∑n=1∞bn(−n2π29−6)sin⁡(nπx3)=6+∑n=1∞2(−1)n+1n3πsin⁡(nπx3).

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain: {−6⋅a02=6bn(−n2π29−6)=2(−1)n+1n3π⇒{a02=−1bn=18(−1)nn3π(n2π2+54)

Therefore, our particular solution is yp∼−1+∑n=1∞18(−1)nn3π(n2π2+54)⋅sin⁡(nπx3).

q-343911.name: Question 11
q-343911.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$
q-343911.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A=4 \\ \pi B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=-\frac{4}{\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=-\frac{4x}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Consider the differential equation y″+π24y=f(x), where the 4-periodic forcing function is given by f(x)∼−2+∑n=1∞4n2sin⁡(nπx2).

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the
n=1

n=2

harmonic of the forcing function. Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form
−4xπcos⁡(πx2)
−8xπcos⁡(πx2)

yp1={(−4xπcos⁡(πx2))(S1)}.

EXPLANATION

We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation

y″+π24y=f(x) has a natural frequency of ω=π24=π2.

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a 4-periodic function (L=2) are ωn=nπ2. For n=1, we have ω1=π2. Since ω1=ω, the n=1 harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the n=1 harmonic, the forcing term is f1(x)=4sin⁡(πx2). Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form yp1=x(Acos⁡(πx2)+Bsin⁡(πx2)).

Now, we compute the derivatives: yp1′=(Acos⁡(πx2)+Bsin⁡(πx2))+x(−π2Asin⁡(πx2)+π2Bcos⁡(πx2))yp1″=−πAsin⁡(πx2)+πBcos⁡(πx2)−π24x(Acos⁡(πx2)+Bsin⁡(πx2))

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp1″ and yp1 into the equation y″+π24y=4sin⁡(πx2): [−πAsin⁡(πx2)+πBcos⁡(πx2)−π24yp1]+π24yp1=4sin⁡(πx2)

The resonant terms involving x cancel out, leaving −πAsin⁡(πx2)+πBcos⁡(πx2)=4sin⁡(πx2).

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain: {−πA=4πB=0⇒{A=−4πB=0

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is yp1=−4xπcos⁡(πx2).

q-343914.name: Question 12
q-343914.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$
q-343914.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}):$

$$
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,[-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4\pi }{3}A=-\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{4\pi }{3}B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=\frac{9}{16\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{9x}{16\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

q-343896.name: Question 13
q-343896.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$
q-343896.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}):$

$$
[-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\pi }{3}A=0 \\ \frac{2\pi }{3}B=1\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{3}{2\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{3x}{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{3}).
$$

q-343891.name: Question 14
q-343891.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $1$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}={{field-2}}.
$$
q-343891.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{36{\pi }^{2}}=6\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $1$-periodic function $(L=\frac{1}{2})$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{(\frac{1}{2})}=2n\pi .
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=6\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x))+x(-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)-36{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x):$

$$
[-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)-36{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+36{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-12\pi A=0 \\ 12\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{108\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{108\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

q-343906.name: Question 15
q-343906.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼4+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{9}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$
q-343906.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $2$-periodic function $(L=1)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{1}=n\pi .
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=9\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=9\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=9\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=9\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A=9 \\ 2\pi B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=-\frac{9}{2\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=-\frac{9x}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).
$$

EXPLANATION

We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation

y″+π2y=f(x) has a natural frequency of ω=π2=π.

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a 2-periodic function (L=1) are ωn=nπ1=nπ. For n=1, we have ω1=π. Since ω1=ω, the n=1 harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the n=1 harmonic, the forcing term is f1(x)=9sin⁡(πx). Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form yp1=x(Acos⁡(πx)+Bsin⁡(πx)).

Now, we compute the derivatives: yp1′=(Acos⁡(πx)+Bsin⁡(πx))+x(−πAsin⁡(πx)+πBcos⁡(πx))yp1″=−2πAsin⁡(πx)+2πBcos⁡(πx)−π2x(Acos⁡(πx)+Bsin⁡(πx))

Next, we substitute the expressions for yp1″ and yp1 into the equation y″+π2y=9sin⁡(πx): [−2πAsin⁡(πx)+2πBcos⁡(πx)−π2yp1]+π2yp1=9sin⁡(πx)

The resonant terms involving x cancel out, leaving −2πAsin⁡(πx)+2πBcos⁡(πx)=9sin⁡(πx).

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain: {−2πA=92πB=0⇒{A=−92πB=0

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is yp1=−9x2πcos⁡(πx).
